newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Euro rand bond issues seen increasing - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Euro rand bond issues seen increasing - bankers.

text.p: The volume of outstanding issues in the Euro rand market is expected to increase while the South African rand is showing signs of steadying, said Hambros Bank Ltd and Rand Merchant Bank Ltd in a joint a presentation to Swiss bankers here.
High yields are likely to attract investors to the sector, said Mark Benstead, director of Hambros Bank Ltd's bond division in London.

"Broad investor appetite suggests a market capital of substantial growth," he said in a presentation, forecasting outstanding issues to rise to between 20 billion to 22 billion rand by end 1997 from nearly 15 billion currently.
Hambros is the largest bookrunner for rand Eurobonds, and Switzerland is the single largest investor market. Hambros works closely with Rand Merchant Bank in the rand bond market.
Hambros has managed nearly half of the nearly 40 Euro rand bonds to have been launched so far in 1997, totaling around 6.1 billion rand, bank officials said.
More than 35 percent of Hambros's Euro rand issues have been distributed in Switzerland, with 23 percent in Austria and Germany, and 17 percent in Benelux and Italy.
The Euro rand sector, which was opened in September 1995, has seen a total of 101 new issues to date.

European investors have been attracted to the sector by comparatively high yields, and the trend has been reinforced as traditional high-yielders like Italy work to conform with membership criteria for European economic and monetary union, bringing their debt levels, and yields lower.

Rudolf Gouws, chief economist at Rand Merchant Bank, expected the outlook for the rand to improve. Although the currency is likely to continue to decline, the rate of decline is seen slowing signficantly.
"We believe the bad news is now over," he said.
"The basic trend in reserves is upward," he added.
Gouws forecast South Africa's foreign currency reserves to rise in 1997 by 4.3 billion rand, after declining by 4.7 billion in 1996.

He also expected the South African central bank to continue to work to bring inflation down, forecasting consumer price inflation at 7.9 percent by year-end 1997, down from 9.4 percent at the end of 1996.
